Nagel.et: From Middle High German nagel, from Old High German nagal, from Proto-West Germanic *nagl.

nagen.et: From Middle High German nagen, from Old High German nagan, gnagan, from Proto-Germanic *gnaganą. Cognate with English nag and gnaw.

Nagetier.et: 18th century, from nagen (“gnaw”) + Tier (“animal”), after earlier Nager, a calque of Latin rodens.

s: to nail (to hammer or drive a nail into something)
to nail (of a male, to have sexual intercourse with a female)
nageln.et: From Middle High German nagelen, from Old High German nagalen, negilen, from Proto-West Germanic *naglijan, from Proto-Germanic *naglijaną. Equivalent to Nagel + -n.

s: only used in niet- und nagelfest

Nagy.et: From Hungarian Nagy, either directly or via Czech Nagy. The meaning is equivalent to native Groß.

s: to act with deliberation, vigour, and professionalism, not waveringly or desultorily

nagelneu.et: From Middle High German nagelniuwe, equivalent to Nagel (“nail”) + neu (“new”) implying a recent manufacture or assembly.

nagut.et: Univerbation of na (“well, so”) + gut (“fine, good”), written as one word due to a shift in the pronunciation to a pattern only used in compounds.

Nagorny Karabach.et: Borrowed from Russian Наго́рный Караба́х (Nagórnyj Karabáx).

s: a surname originating as an occupation

Nagelprobe.et: From Nagel + Probe, referring to the Daumennagel (“thumbnail”).

s: nail wedge resection, partial nail avulsion (minor surgical procedure that involves the removal of a small strip of the side of the nail and the destruction of a section of the nail matrix)
